requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate' have been reproduced, including the MSE-optimal and inner-product-optimal quantizers, their theoretical distortion bounds, and their empirical performance on KV cache compression and nearest-neighbor search.

The random rotation matrix (via QR decomposition of a Gaussian matrix), the observation of Beta-distributed coordinates on the rotated unit sphere, and the optimal Lloyd-Max scalar codebook precomputation for the Beta/Gaussian distribution are implemented as described in Section 3.1 and Lemma 1.
The random rotation matrix Π used to whiten worst-case inputs is constructed via QR decomposition of a Gaussian matrix and used identically by Quant and DeQuant.
Code has been implemented that generates a d×d matrix G with i.i.d. entries drawn from N(0,1) as the input to the QR-based rotation construction (Section 3.1).
Code has been implemented that produces the rotation matrix Π by applying QR decomposition to the Gaussian matrix and taking the orthogonal Q factor (line 2 of Algorithm 1).
The generated rotation matrix Π satisfies Π·Π^T = I to within numerical tolerance (e.g. max |Π·Π^T - I| < 1e-4), confirming orthogonality of the QR-derived rotation.
Quant_mse uses y = Π·x (line 5 of Algorithm 1) and DeQuant_mse uses x̃ = Π^T·ỹ (line 10) so that the identical Π (a persisted global parameter of the quantizer) is used in both directions.

For any unit vector x on S^{d-1}, the empirical distribution of Π·x across many draws of Π is uniform on the unit hypersphere, verified by checking that the empirical mean of ‖Π·x‖ is 1 and that the coordinate marginals are symmetric around 0 with variance ≈ 1/d.

The Beta-distribution characterisation of coordinates of a uniformly random point on the hypersphere (Lemma 1) is implemented and empirically validated, including the high-dimensional convergence to N(0, 1/d).

Code has been implemented that evaluates the pdf f_X(x) = Γ(d/2)/(√π · Γ((d-1)/2)) · (1 - x^2)^((d-3)/2) on x ∈ [-1, 1] as given by Lemma 1, used as the source distribution for the scalar-quantizer solver.

For a fixed d (e.g. d = 1536), the empirical histogram of coordinates of Π·x for a random unit vector matches the Lemma-1 Beta density f_X within a Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic below 0.02 over ≥ 10^5 samples.

For large d (e.g. d ≥ 512), the empirical variance of a single coordinate of Π·x, averaged over many rotations of a unit vector, is 1/d to within 5% relative tolerance, confirming convergence of the Beta distribution to N(0, 1/d).

The Lloyd-Max / Max-Lloyd solver for the optimal 1-D scalar quantizer of the Beta (or Gaussian) source distribution is implemented, and the resulting codebooks are precomputed and cached across a range of bit-widths per Eq. (4).

Code has been implemented for an iterative continuous 1-D k-means / Max-Lloyd routine that, given a source density f_X and a bit-width b, returns 2^b centroids minimizing the MSE cost C(f_X, b) of Eq. (4).

The solver enforces the Voronoi-tessellation optimality condition: consecutive interval boundaries used to compute the integrals in Eq. (4) equal the midpoints (c_i + c_{i+1})/2 of adjacent sorted centroids.

The Max-Lloyd solver runs to numerical convergence (successive-iterate MSE change below a fixed tolerance such as 1e-8) so that returned codebooks are stationary points of the k-means objective in Eq. (4).

Code has been implemented that precomputes and stores (on disk or in-module) the optimal Lloyd-Max codebooks {c_1,...,c_{2^b}} for a range of practically relevant bit-widths (at least b = 1, 2, 3, 4), so subsequent Quant/DeQuant calls do not re-solve Eq. (4).
For b = 1 and large d, the precomputed codebook consists of exactly the two centroids ±√(2/(πd)) as stated in Section 3.1, matching the Gaussian-limit optimum to within 2% relative error.
For b = 2, the four precomputed centroids are symmetric around zero and match the values displayed in Section 3.1 for the N(0, 1/d) limit within 5% relative error.

Code has been implemented that, for bit-widths b > 4, falls back to the Panter–Dite high-resolution formula C(f_X, b) ≤ (√3π/2) · 4^{-b} / d instead of running the numerical Max-Lloyd solver, matching the tail bound used to prove Theorem 1.

The numerically computed optimal per-coordinate MSE cost C(f_X, 1) equals 0.36/d within 5% relative tolerance for the Beta/Gaussian source, matching the value quoted for b = 1 in Section 3.1 and used in Theorem 1.
The numerically computed optimal per-coordinate MSE cost C(f_X, 2) equals 0.117/d within 5% relative tolerance for the Beta/Gaussian source, matching the value quoted for b = 2 in Section 3.1.
The numerically computed optimal per-coordinate MSE cost C(f_X, 3) equals 0.03/d within 10% relative tolerance for the Beta/Gaussian source, matching the value quoted for b = 3 in Section 3.1.
The numerically computed optimal per-coordinate MSE cost C(f_X, 4) equals 0.009/d within 15% relative tolerance for the Beta/Gaussian source, matching the value quoted for b = 4 in Section 3.1.
The per-coordinate nearest-centroid encoder/decoder that consumes the precomputed codebook is implemented as lines 6 and 9 of Algorithm 1.
Code has been implemented that, per coordinate j of Π·x, returns the argmin_{k ∈ [2^b]} |y_j - c_k| index, packing the result into a d-length b-bit integer tensor as in line 6 of Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented that reconstructs ỹ_j = c_{idx_j} from the stored index vector and precomputed codebook (line 9 of Algorithm 1), returning the same dtype/shape expected by the subsequent Π^T multiplication.

The 1-bit QJL primitive from Definition 1 (random Gaussian projection matrix S, sign quantization, and rescaled dequantization via S^T) is implemented with the unbiasedness and variance guarantees stated in Lemma 4, so it can serve as the second-stage residual quantizer for TurboQuant_prod.
The QJL primitive is implemented as a self-contained module exposing quantization and dequantization procedures matching Definition 1.

Code has been implemented that defines a QJL module (e.g., a class or a pair of functions Quant_qjl and DeQuant_qjl) parameterized by input dimension d, matching the signature Q_qjl: R^d -> {-1,+1}^d and Q_qjl^{-1}: {-1,+1}^d -> R^d in Definition 1.
Code has been implemented that constructs the random projection matrix S in R^{d x d} with entries sampled i.i.d. from N(0, 1) at instantiation time, in accordance with Definition 1.

The same random matrix S (or an equivalent seeded RNG) is persisted between calls to Quant_qjl and DeQuant_qjl on the same QJL instance so that quantize/dequantize round-trips are consistent, and this state is exposed for reuse by TurboQuant_prod.
Quant_qjl and DeQuant_qjl implement the exact mathematical operations of Definition 1 with correct scaling.
Quant_qjl computes sign(S @ x) applied entry-wise so that for any input x in R^d the output is a length-d vector whose i-th entry is sign((S x)_i).
For any test input x in R^d, the returned quantized vector from Quant_qjl contains only values in {-1, +1} and has length d.

DeQuant_qjl reconstructs a d-dim real vector by multiplying the quantized {-1,+1} vector by S^T with the paper's normalization (sqrt(pi*d/2) / d = sqrt(pi/(2d)) scaling) so that <y, DeQuant_qjl(Quant_qjl(x))> is an unbiased estimator of <y, x> as stated in Definition 1 and Lemma 4.
Composing Quant_qjl then DeQuant_qjl on a unit-norm x in R^d returns a real-valued vector of shape (d,) whose L2 norm is finite and non-zero (sanity that no dimension collapse occurred).
Empirical validation of Lemma 4's unbiasedness statement: E[<y, Q_qjl^{-1}(Q_qjl(x))>] = <y, x> for any x on the unit sphere and any y in R^d.

Code has been implemented that runs a Monte Carlo experiment which draws many independent instances of S, computes the QJL inner-product estimator <y, Q_qjl^{-1}(Q_qjl(x))> for a fixed x on the unit sphere and a fixed y in R^d, and returns the empirical mean and variance across trials.

In the Monte Carlo experiment above, the absolute bias |E_hat[<y, Q_qjl^{-1}(Q_qjl(x))>] - <y, x>| is within Monte Carlo tolerance of zero (e.g., within 3 standard errors of the mean) across multiple randomly chosen (x, y) pairs with x on the unit sphere, matching the unbiasedness guarantee of Lemma 4.
Empirical validation of Lemma 4's variance guarantee: Var[<y, Q_qjl^{-1}(Q_qjl(x))>] <= (pi/2) * ||y||^2 / d for any x on the unit sphere and any y in R^d.

Code has been implemented that reports the empirical variance of the QJL inner-product estimator across Monte Carlo trials alongside the theoretical bound (pi/2) * ||y||^2 / d for the same (x, y) inputs.

The measured empirical variance of the QJL inner-product estimator satisfies Var_hat[<y, Q_qjl^{-1}(Q_qjl(x))>] <= (pi/2) * ||y||^2 / d (within Monte Carlo tolerance) for x on the unit sphere and multiple choices of y in R^d, reproducing the variance bound of Lemma 4.
The QJL primitive is exposed and reused by the inner-product-optimal TurboQuant algorithm (Algorithm 2) rather than reimplemented inline.

The TurboQuant_prod implementation (Algorithm 2) imports and calls the QJL Quant_qjl / DeQuant_qjl (or the underlying sign(S*r) and sqrt(pi*d/2)*S^T*qjl operations) from this QJL module for the residual quantization step described in Section 3.2.

A standalone unit test exercises the QJL module in isolation (independent of TurboQuant_mse and TurboQuant_prod), constructing a small (d, S, x, y) instance and asserting shape, {-1,+1} output domain, and the Definition-1 dequantization formula on hand-computed inputs.

The MSE-optimal TurboQuant algorithm (Algorithm 1) is fully implemented, including Quant_mse (random rotation + nearest-centroid indexing) and DeQuant_mse (centroid lookup + inverse rotation), with the Lloyd-Max codebooks for practically relevant bit-widths b=1..8. The implementation must expose the Quant_mse / DeQuant_mse primitives, produce indices in [2^b]^d, be vectorized on the GPU, and match the paper's small-bit MSE distortion numbers on unit-sphere inputs.
The Lloyd-Max codebook design that solves Eq. (4) for the (shifted/scaled) Beta density fX from Lemma 1 is implemented and precomputed offline for the bit-widths used by TurboQuant_mse.

Code has been implemented for a 1-D Lloyd-Max / continuous k-means solver that partitions [-1, 1] into 2^b clusters with respect to a supplied source density (the Beta density fX(x) = (1/(sqrt(pi)) * Gamma(d/2)/Gamma((d-1)/2)) * (1-x^2)^((d-3)/2) or its Gaussian N(0, 1/d) approximation).

Code has been implemented for evaluating the coordinate density fX(x) from Lemma 1 (Beta distribution on the sphere) and/or its N(0, 1/d) limit, which is fed to the Lloyd-Max solver as the source distribution.
The Lloyd-Max update computes cluster boundaries as midpoints between consecutive sorted centroids (Voronoi tessellation of the real line), matching the optimality condition described in Section 3.1.

The Lloyd-Max update recomputes each centroid c_i as the conditional expectation E[X | X in bucket_i] under the source density fX, i.e. c_i = (integral over bucket of x*fX dx) / (integral over bucket of fX dx).

The Lloyd-Max solver iterates the boundary / centroid updates until the MSE cost C(fX, b) in Eq. (4) converges (change below a tolerance or max-iterations reached) and returns the final sorted centroid vector.
For b=1 in the moderate-to-high-d regime, the optimal centroids returned by the Lloyd-Max solver equal +/- sqrt(2/(pi*d)) (up to numerical tolerance), matching the closed form quoted in Section 3.1.
Codebooks are precomputed once (offline) and stored on disk / in a module-level constant for every bit-width b in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; no Lloyd-Max iteration runs at Quant_mse call time.

A loader utility reads the precomputed codebook for the requested (d, b) and returns a sorted tensor of length 2^b that Quant_mse uses; the loader raises a clear error if b is outside the supported 1..8 range.

The precomputed codebooks are symmetric around 0 (for every centroid c, -c is also a centroid) and the numerical MSE cost C(fX, b) is monotonically decreasing in b, matching the well-known Lloyd-Max properties.
The Quant_mse procedure (Algorithm 1 lines 4-7): random-rotate the input vector and, per coordinate, output the index of the nearest Lloyd-Max centroid.

Code has been implemented for a callable/class `Quant_mse` that takes a d-dimensional (or batch of d-dimensional) input vector x and a bit-width b and returns an integer index tensor of shape (..., d) with values in [0, 2^b).
Quant_mse computes y = Pi @ x using the shared random rotation matrix Pi (built once at algorithm instantiation) before the coordinate-wise indexing step, matching line 5 of Algorithm 1.

For each coordinate j, Quant_mse selects idx_j = argmin_{k in [2^b]} |y_j - c_k| against the loaded codebook, matching line 6 of Algorithm 1; a unit test with a hand-picked y and codebook confirms the correct indices are returned.

The nearest-centroid search is implemented in a vectorized/batched fashion (e.g. torch bucketize / searchsorted or a fused kernel) rather than a per-coordinate Python loop, so Quant_mse can run over batches of d-dimensional vectors on a single GPU.

The returned index tensor uses an integer dtype wide enough to hold b bits (e.g. uint8 for b<=8) and the total encoded footprint is exactly b*d bits per vector, matching the target bit-width contract of the paper.

A behavioral test constructs a synthetic input whose rotated coordinates land arbitrarily close to specific centroids and confirms Quant_mse returns exactly those centroids' indices for every coordinate.
The DeQuant_mse procedure (Algorithm 1 lines 8-11): look up centroids from indices and apply the inverse rotation.
Code has been implemented for a callable/class `DeQuant_mse` that takes an index tensor of shape (..., d) (values in [0, 2^b)) and returns a reconstructed real-valued vector of shape (..., d).
DeQuant_mse first performs y_tilde_j = c_{idx_j} (a plain gather / take on the codebook tensor) for every coordinate j, matching line 9 of Algorithm 1.
DeQuant_mse then computes x_tilde = Pi^T @ y_tilde using the transpose of the same rotation matrix stored at instantiation, matching line 10 of Algorithm 1.

A behavioral test verifies that for random unit-norm x, DeQuant_mse(Quant_mse(x)) at b=8 reconstructs x with L2 reconstruction error less than 0.1 (i.e. round-trip loss shrinks quickly with b as expected from Theorem 1).
End-to-end plumbing and API expected of Algorithm 1: deterministic given a seed, exposes both Quant and DeQuant primitives, handles non-unit-norm inputs via stored norms, and runs on GPU.

The TurboQuant_mse setup is deterministic given a fixed random seed: two instantiations with the same seed produce identical rotation matrices Pi and therefore Quant_mse produces identical indices on the same input.

The implementation exposes the paper's `Quant` and `DeQuant` primitives (Section 1.1) at the module level so a dataset x_1, ..., x_n can be quantized in bulk and each vector individually reconstructed via Q^{-1}(Q(x_i)).

For non-unit-norm inputs, code has been implemented that stores the per-vector L2 norm in floating point alongside the index tensor and rescales the DeQuant_mse output by that norm, as described in the remark following Theorem 1.
Both Quant_mse and DeQuant_mse execute end-to-end on a CUDA tensor input without dropping to CPU inside their hot path, consistent with the paper's claim of GPU/vectorization friendliness.
Empirical MSE distortion D_mse = E[||x - DeQuant_mse(Quant_mse(x))||_2^2] measured for random unit-norm x in R^d matches the small-bit-width values quoted in Theorem 1 for b = 1, 2, 3, 4.

Measured D_mse at bit-width b=1, averaged over many random unit-norm x and rotation seeds in sufficiently high dimension d, equals approximately 0.36 (matching the number quoted for b=1 in Theorem 1).
Measured D_mse at bit-width b=2, averaged over many random unit-norm x and rotation seeds, equals approximately 0.117 (matching the number quoted for b=2 in Theorem 1).
Measured D_mse at bit-width b=3, averaged over many random unit-norm x and rotation seeds, equals approximately 0.03 (matching the number quoted for b=3 in Theorem 1).
Measured D_mse at bit-width b=4, averaged over many random unit-norm x and rotation seeds, equals approximately 0.009 (matching the number quoted for b=4 in Theorem 1).

sub_tasks.requirements: The inner-product-optimal TurboQuant algorithm (Algorithm 2) is fully implemented as a two-stage composition of TurboQuant_mse (with bit-width b-1) on the input followed by QJL on the residual, producing (idx, qjl, ||r||_2) triples that yield unbiased inner-product estimates.

The global initialization for TurboQuant_prod (Algorithm 2 lines 2-3) is implemented: it instantiates a TurboQuant_mse quantizer with bit-width b-1 and generates a random projection matrix S with i.i.d. N(0,1) entries.

Code has been implemented that constructs a TurboQuant_prod instance which internally instantiates a TurboQuant_mse quantizer configured with bit-width b-1 (one less than the caller-requested bit-width b).

Code has been implemented that samples a projection matrix S of shape (d, d) with entries drawn i.i.d. from the standard normal distribution N(0, 1), and stores S as a persistent global parameter of the quantizer.

The random projection matrix S has empirical column-mean approximately 0 and empirical entry-variance approximately 1 (checked by sampling a large S and confirming |mean| < 0.02 and |variance - 1| < 0.05).

Code has been implemented so that when TurboQuant_prod is constructed with bit-width b=1, the internal TurboQuant_mse is used with bit-width 0 (i.e. Quant_mse returns no indices and its dequantization returns the zero vector), leaving qjl to carry the entire bit budget.
The Quant_prod procedure (Algorithm 2 lines 4-8) is implemented as a two-stage encoder that produces the triple (idx, qjl, ||r||_2).

Code has been implemented for a callable procedure Quant_prod(x) that accepts a d-dimensional vector x and returns a triple whose first element is an integer index array, second element is a {-1, +1}-valued sign array, and third element is a nonnegative scalar.
Quant_prod computes its idx output by delegating to the internal Quant_mse(x) call from Algorithm 1 at bit-width b-1; the returned indices lie in [0, 2^(b-1)) elementwise.
Quant_prod computes the residual vector r = x - DeQuant_mse(idx) using the same rotation matrix Pi and codebook as the internal TurboQuant_mse, and unit tests verify r has the same shape as x.

For a unit-norm input x with the mse codebook and Pi held fixed, the residual r produced by Quant_prod satisfies ||r||_2^2 numerically equal to ||x||_2^2 - ||DeQuant_mse(idx)||_2^2 up to floating-point error of 1e-5, confirming the residual is the arithmetic difference and not a re-quantized approximation.
Quant_prod computes qjl = sign(S @ r) where S is the stored d x d N(0,1) projection matrix, and the output is a length-d array whose entries are all in {-1, +1}.

Quant_prod stores the L2 norm gamma = ||r||_2 of the residual (as a floating-point scalar) alongside idx and qjl in its output triple; a unit test constructs a residual with known norm and confirms the stored gamma matches to 1e-6.

The total serialized bit-width of the Quant_prod output is b*d: idx contributes (b-1)*d bits (d indices of (b-1) bits each) and qjl contributes d bits, matching the b*d budget stated in Theorem 2 (the O(1) bits for gamma are stored separately as a floating-point rescale factor).
The DeQuant_prod procedure (Algorithm 2 lines 9-12) is implemented and reconstructs x_tilde as the sum of DeQuant_mse(idx) and the QJL rescaled inverse sqrt(pi*d/2) * gamma * S^T @ qjl.
Code has been implemented for a callable DeQuant_prod(idx, qjl, gamma) procedure that accepts the triple emitted by Quant_prod and returns a d-dimensional reconstructed vector.

DeQuant_prod first reconstructs x_tilde_mse via DeQuant_mse(idx) using the same Pi and codebook as during quantization; a round-trip unit test with gamma=0 (residual set to zero manually) shows the output equals DeQuant_mse(idx).

DeQuant_prod computes the QJL contribution as x_tilde_qjl = sqrt(pi * d / 2) * gamma * (S^T @ qjl), using the same S matrix that was used during quantization; the scalar prefactor is exactly sqrt(pi*d/2), verified numerically to 1e-6.

DeQuant_prod returns x_tilde_mse + x_tilde_qjl (elementwise sum of the two d-dimensional reconstructions); a unit test verifies this composition rather than any weighted average or replacement of one term.

The outlier/non-outlier channel splitting strategy is implemented: 32 outlier channels at 3 bits + 96 regular channels at 2 bits => effective 2.5 bits/channel, with a corresponding split producing effective 3.5 bits/channel, using two independent TurboQuant instances as described in Section 4.3.

Outlier channels are identified per attention head so that a fixed number of high-magnitude channels can be routed to a higher-bit quantizer, following the outlier-aware treatment of Section 4.3 (consistent with prior work RotateKV / QJL cited as [63, 51]).

Code has been implemented that, given a batch of key/value channel activations of head-dim 128, selects a configurable number of channels to be treated as outliers (e.g., by activation magnitude or a precomputed channel-index list) and returns the complementary set as regular channels.

Code has been implemented so that the 2.5-bit configuration selects exactly 32 outlier channels and 96 regular channels out of a 128-dimensional head, and the partitioning is stable/deterministic across calls (i.e., the selected index set does not change between token steps for a given head).
Two independent TurboQuant instances are used, one for the outlier sub-vector and one for the regular sub-vector, each with its own randomness and bit-width, as described in Section 4.3.

Code has been implemented that instantiates two separate TurboQuant quantizer objects (Algorithm 1 or Algorithm 2) — one operating on the outlier sub-vector and one on the regular sub-vector — rather than reusing a single instance for both.

Code has been implemented so that the two TurboQuant instances hold independently sampled random rotation matrices Π (and, for TurboQuant_prod, independent QJL projection matrices S) sized to the outlier sub-dim (32) and regular sub-dim (96) respectively; a test asserts the two rotation matrices are not identical.

Code has been implemented so that the outlier instance quantizes at 3 bits per coordinate and the regular instance quantizes at 2 bits per coordinate for the 2.5-bit configuration, verified by inspecting the codebook size (2^3 = 8 for outliers, 2^2 = 4 for regulars) of each instance.
The 2.5-bit non-integer bit-width configuration is implemented via 32 outlier channels at 3 bits and 96 regular channels at 2 bits on a 128-dim head.

Code has been implemented that exposes a named configuration (e.g., `turboquant_2p5bit`) which wires the outlier selector, the 3-bit outlier TurboQuant, the 2-bit regular TurboQuant, and the reassembly logic into a single quantize/dequantize entry point over the full 128-dim head.

The 2.5-bit configuration is verified to have effective bit precision equal to (32 * 3 + 96 * 2) / 128 = 2.5 bits/channel: a test computes the total bits emitted by Quant on a single 128-dim head vector and divides by 128, and the resulting value matches 2.5 exactly (integer-bit accounting, no metadata).
The 3.5-bit non-integer bit-width configuration is implemented with a correspondingly higher-precision split of outlier vs. regular channels (Section 4.3).

Code has been implemented that exposes a `turboquant_3p5bit` configuration whose per-channel bit assignment (e.g., outlier channels at 4 bits and regular channels at 3 bits, with the ratio chosen so the weighted average is 3.5) is documented in the source and produced by the same two-instance splitting mechanism used for 2.5 bits.

The 3.5-bit configuration is verified to have effective bit precision equal to 3.5 bits/channel on a 128-dim head: a test computes total emitted bits per head divided by 128 and matches 3.5 exactly for the chosen outlier/regular split.

The dequantization path reassembles the outlier and regular sub-vectors back into a full-dimensional vector at their original channel indices so downstream attention consumes a tensor of the original shape.

Code has been implemented that scatters the dequantized outlier coordinates and dequantized regular coordinates back into their original 128-dim channel positions using the outlier index set from the selector, producing a single output tensor.

A behavioral test feeds a random unit-norm 128-dim vector through the 2.5-bit split-quantize -> split-dequantize pipeline and asserts (a) the output has shape (128,) with no NaNs, and (b) the MSE against the input is finite and lower than a same-bit-budget uniform 2-bit TurboQuant applied to the whole vector (confirming the outlier channels really do get more bits).
